-- Monthly overdue report for a fictional city library (sample script, Oracle)
-- Written over the years by several people; Amber shows what it really does.
SET SERVEROUTPUT ON
DEFINE report_month = '2026-10'

CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_overdue (
  loan_id    NUMBER,
  member_id  NUMBER,
  branch_id  NUMBER,
  days_late  NUMBER
) ON COMMIT PRESERVE ROWS;

INSERT INTO tmp_overdue (loan_id, member_id, branch_id, days_late)
SELECT l.loan_id, l.member_id, b.branch_id, TRUNC(SYSDATE) - l.due_on
  FROM lib.loans l, lib.copies c, lib.branches b
 WHERE l.copy_id = c.copy_id
   AND c.branch_id = b.branch_id
   AND l.returned_on IS NULL
   AND TO_CHAR(l.due_on, 'YYYY-MM') <= '&report_month';

-- old fee rule: 0.25 per day, capped by member category
MERGE INTO lib.member_fees f
USING (
  SELECT o.member_id,
         SUM(LEAST(o.days_late * 0.25, NVL(m.fee_cap, 10))) AS fee
    FROM tmp_overdue o
    LEFT JOIN lib.members m ON m.member_id = o.member_id
   WHERE m.status = 'ACTIVE'
   GROUP BY o.member_id
) x
ON (f.member_id = x.member_id AND f.period = '&report_month')
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET f.amount = x.fee, f.updated_on = SYSDATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (member_id, period, amount, updated_on)
  VALUES (x.member_id, '&report_month', x.fee, SYSDATE);

BEGIN
  FOR r IN (SELECT branch_id, COUNT(*) cnt FROM tmp_overdue GROUP BY branch_id) LOOP
    UPDATE lib.branches SET overdue_count = r.cnt WHERE branch_id = r.branch_id;
    COMMIT;
  END LOOP;
EXCEPTION
  WHEN OTHERS THEN
    ROLLBACK;
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('branch update failed: ' || SQLERRM);
END;
/

-- branch hierarchy with overdue totals per region
SELECT LPAD(' ', 2 * (LEVEL - 1)) || b.name AS branch,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tmp_overdue o WHERE o.branch_id = b.branch_id) AS overdue
  FROM lib.branches b
 START WITH b.parent_id IS NULL
CONNECT BY PRIOR b.branch_id = b.parent_id;

SELECT *
  FROM (SELECT m.member_id, m.display_name, f.amount
          FROM lib.members m
          JOIN lib.member_fees f ON f.member_id = m.member_id
         WHERE f.period = '&report_month'
           AND m.member_id NOT IN (SELECT member_id FROM lib.fee_waivers)
         ORDER BY f.amount DESC)
 WHERE ROWNUM <= 20;

DROP TABLE tmp_overdue PURGE;

findings.title: Function on a filtered column
findings.message: TO_CHAR(…) is applied to a column before comparing it; an index on that column cannot be used.
findings.suggestion: Compare the bare column with a transformed value (e.g. a date range instead of TRUNC(col)).

findings.title: LEFT JOIN behaves as INNER JOIN
findings.message: The WHERE condition on m.status drops the rows the LEFT JOIN kept.
findings.suggestion: Move the condition into the ON clause, or use INNER JOIN if that is intended.

findings.title: Row-by-row DML in a loop
findings.message: This update runs once per loop iteration.
findings.suggestion: Replace the loop with one set-based statement (INSERT … SELECT, UPDATE … FROM, MERGE), or batch it (FORALL / bulk binds).

findings.title: COMMIT inside a loop
findings.message: Committing every iteration is slow and leaves partial results if the loop fails.
findings.suggestion: Commit once after the loop, or in larger batches.

findings.title: NOT IN with a subquery
findings.message: If the subquery returns a NULL, NOT IN matches no rows.
findings.suggestion: Use NOT EXISTS, or filter NULLs out of the subquery.

rewrites.title: LEFT JOIN → JOIN
rewrites.explanation: The WHERE condition m.status = 'ACTIVE' is never true for the rows the LEFT JOIN adds when m has no match (their columns are NULL), so those rows are filtered out and the join already behaves as an inner join. Writing JOIN says so. If the outer join was intended, move the condition into the ON clause instead.
rewrites.rewrittenStatement:
MERGE INTO lib.member_fees f
USING (
  SELECT o.member_id,
         SUM(LEAST(o.days_late * 0.25, NVL(m.fee_cap, 10))) AS fee
    FROM tmp_overdue o
    JOIN lib.members m ON m.member_id = o.member_id
   WHERE m.status = 'ACTIVE'
   GROUP BY o.member_id
) x
ON (f.member_id = x.member_id AND f.period = '&report_month')
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET f.amount = x.fee, f.updated_on = SYSDATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (member_id, period, amount, updated_on)
  VALUES (x.member_id, '&report_month', x.fee, SYSDATE)
rewrites.safetyNote: The WHERE condition rejects NULL, so the result is the same for any data.

rewrites.title: NOT IN (subquery) → NOT EXISTS
rewrites.explanation: NOT IN with a subquery returns no rows at all as soon as the subquery yields one NULL. NOT EXISTS with the same condition written as a correlation (member_id = m.member_id) states the intent: keep the rows that have no match.
rewrites.rewrittenStatement:
SELECT *
  FROM (SELECT m.member_id, m.display_name, f.amount
          FROM lib.members m
          JOIN lib.member_fees f ON f.member_id = m.member_id
         WHERE f.period = '&report_month'
           AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM lib.fee_waivers WHERE member_id = m.member_id)
         ORDER BY f.amount DESC)
 WHERE ROWNUM <= 20
rewrites.safetyNote: Differs when NULLs occur: m.member_id NOT IN (SELECT member_id FROM lib.fee_waivers) returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL member_id, and never keeps a row whose m.member_id is NULL; NOT EXISTS ignores the NULL and keeps such rows. That is usually the intended behavior. Their nullability is not known (add metadata to prove both NOT NULL).
